title: India Sweeps Five Golds at the World's First Yogasana Championship. The Sport Is Chasing Olympic Recognition.
excerpt: More than 400 athletes from 60 countries competed in Ahmedabad. India's dominance was total from the opening day.
body:
India announced itself as the undisputed global force in competitive Yogasana this week, sweeping five of the first six gold medals at the inaugural World Yogasana Championships 2026 in Ahmedabad. The event, running June 4 to 8 at the Eka Arena, is the largest international platform ever built for Yogasana as a competitive sport, and it arrives just two weeks before International Day of Yoga on June 21.

More than 400 athletes from over 60 countries are competing across six age categories, from Sub-Juniors (10-14) to Senior C (45-55). India has fielded a 122-member contingent, and on the opening day, its athletes made the scale of their advantage clear.

## The Gold Rush

West Bengal's Abhay Burman won India's first gold medal of the Championships in the Traditional Yogasana Senior Male category, scoring 63.42 points — more than six points ahead of Indonesia's Arkan Riyanto, who took silver with 57.23. Uzbekistan's Alan claimed bronze with 53.21.

"Winning the first gold medal of the inaugural World Yogasana Championships for India is a moment I will cherish forever," Burman said. "Competing at home in front of such passionate supporters gave me immense confidence."

Ritu Mondal followed with gold in the Senior Female category, scoring 64.33 points. Kazakhstan's Aizhan Kuanyshbayeva took silver (58.97), while Hong Kong's Lam Nga Man earned bronze (56.98). Mondal, who began training at 12 and won at 20, called it "a landmark moment for every Yogasana athlete."

The only gold India missed was the Senior A Male event, where Singapore's Nathaniel Tan Leong An edged ahead with 55.37 points. India's Sumir Gnawali settled for bronze. But the hosts quickly recovered: Ritu Thakur won Senior A Female (63.50), Roshan Thapa took Senior B Male with the highest individual score of the day (65.67), and Jyoti Deurkar claimed Senior B Female (46.14).

## The Olympic Question

The Championships are backed by India's Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports, the Ministry of Ayush, Sports Authority of India, and Gujarat's state sports authority. Prime Minister Narendra Modi addressed participants virtually at the opening ceremony, calling the event "a new chapter in the global sports landscape."

The organisers have made no secret of their ambition: they want Yogasana recognised as an Olympic discipline. The inaugural championship is designed to build the institutional framework, international participation records, and competitive infrastructure that the International Olympic Committee requires before considering new sports.

## Yoga for Healthy Ageing

The timing is deliberate. International Day of Yoga, observed worldwide on June 21, carries the 2026 theme "Yoga for Healthy Ageing." India's Ministry of Ayush announced the theme, highlighting yoga's role in improving not just lifespan but "healthspan" — the years spent free from chronic disease and disability.

The science supports the emphasis. Research publications on yoga and healthy ageing indexed on PubMed Central have grown from 183 in 2014 to over 1,200 by 2025, a six-fold increase. Clinical studies show regular yoga practice reduces cortisol levels, improves sleep quality, and maintains mobility and balance in older adults.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

For the estimated 18 million members of the Indian diaspora in the US alone, yoga has long been both a cultural heritage and a practical wellness tool. Community centres, temples, and Indian cultural associations across North America, the UK, and the Gulf states hold yoga sessions year-round, and participation surges around International Yoga Day.

The Championship adds a competitive dimension that could reshape how the next generation engages with the practice. If Yogasana gains Olympic recognition, it would join a very short list of sports with roots in Indian tradition on the world's biggest stage.

Indian consulates worldwide are already planning events for June 21. Last week, the Indian Consulate in New York hosted a Yoga Cruise on the East River, with participants performing asanas against the backdrop of the Statue of Liberty and Brooklyn Bridge. Consul General Binaya Srikanta Pradhan called yoga "a holistic approach to well-being that transcends geographical and cultural boundaries."

The main global event this year will be held in Kolkata, but the message from Ahmedabad is broader: India is not just exporting yoga as a lifestyle practice. It is building the infrastructure to turn it into a global sport.
